items.readable_text:
Content:
Let's consider a concrete example of sinusoidal motion in context.

Content:
Suppose a nut is mounted on a vehicle's wheel, and the wheel is stuck in some mud, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4c79f4dbaa64d06b46ee060e0f95c364]

Content:
Let's assume that the wheel rotates at a constant rate. Then the distance from the nut to the ground, in inches, can be modeled by a sinusoidal function [MATH: H(t),] where [MATH: t] is the time in seconds. The graph of [MATH: H(t)] is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/cc720d8d9572a60860ea9e5d9a72b24f]

Content:
Note that negative values of [MATH: H] mean the nut is under the mud.

Content:
We can obtain the following information from the graph:

Content:
- The midline is given by the line [MATH: H=10.] This means the center of the wheel is located [MATH: 10\:\textrm{cm}] above the ground.
- The nut reaches a distance of [MATH: 35 \: \textrm{cm}] above the ground at its highest point and [MATH: 15 \: \textrm{cm}] into the mud at its lowest point.
- The amplitude is [MATH: 35-10 = 25 \: \textrm{cm},] and it represents the distance from the nut to the center of the wheel.
- The period is [MATH: 5 - 1 = 4 \: \textrm{s},] and it tells us that the wheel makes one full rotation every [MATH: 4] seconds.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/2d2909b4e5799f749426b41bebc8130d]

items.title: Interpreting a Cosine Function

sections.normalized_html: The daily tide level in a coastal city, in feet, is modeled by the function [MATH: H(t)=6\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\right)+ 8,] where [MATH: t] is the time in hours. How long does it take for the tide to transition from its lowest to highest level, and what is the maximum height of the tide?
sections.readable_text:
The daily tide level in a coastal city, in feet, is modeled by the function
[MATH: H(t)=6\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\right)+ 8,]
where [MATH: t] is the time in hours. How long does it take for the tide to transition from its lowest to highest level, and what is the maximum height of the tide?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let's recall the general terminology for sinusoidal curves:

If [MATH: F(t) = A \cos\left( B t \right) + C,] then

  • [MATH: |A|] is the amplitude,

  • [MATH: \dfrac{|B|}{2\pi}] is the frequency, [MATH: \dfrac{2\pi}{|B|}] is the period, and

  • [MATH: C] is the midline (vertical shift).

We'll answer each part of the question in turn.

  • For the first part, we are interested in the time difference between the highest and lowest tides (i.e., half the period of the function).

    Now, we have [MATH: B = (π)/(6).] So, the period is [MATH: (2π)/(B)|= (2π)/(((π)/(6))); = 12hr.] The time between the lowest and highest tides is half the period. Therefore, it takes [MATH: 6] hours for the tide to transition from its lowest to highest level.

  • For the second part, we're interested in the maximum value of the function. This is given by the amplitude plus the midline.

    Now, we have [MATH: |A| = 6\,\textrm{ft}, \qquad C = 8\,\textrm{ft}.] Therefore, [MATH: H_{\textrm{max}} = 6\,\textrm{ft} + 8\,\textrm{ft} = 14\,\textrm{ft}.] Therefore, the maximum height of the tide is [MATH: 14\,\textrm{ft}.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Trigonometric functions, or more precisely, sinusoidal curves of the form

Content:
[MATH: F(t) = A \sin(Bt) + C]

Content:
or

Content:
[MATH: G(t) = A \cos(Bt) + C]

Content:
can be used to model real-world processes that are periodic in time [MATH: t.]

Content:
We use the word "sinusoidal" to refer to either sine or cosine. A sketch of a typical sinusoidal curve is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/97503a0f416c5b51a37ca0c37af5d029]

Content:
Now, let's recall some terminology related to sinusoidal functions:

Content:
- The horizontal line that splits the graph in half is called the midline. It corresponds to the vertical shift [MATH: C] of the function.
- The distance from the midline to the highest (or lowest) position is called the amplitude.
[MATH: \textrm{amplitude} = |A|]
- The period tells us how much time must elapse before the process repeats. The period can be calculated using the formula
[MATH: \textrm{period} = \dfrac{2\pi}{|B|}.]
- The reciprocal of the period is called the frequency. It shows how many times the process repeats per unit of time.
[MATH: \textrm{frequency} = \dfrac{|B|}{2\pi}]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: A Sinusoidal Model of a Rotating Wheel Nut

Content:
Let's consider a concrete example of sinusoidal motion in context.

Content:
Suppose a nut is mounted on a vehicle's wheel, and the wheel is stuck in some mud, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4c79f4dbaa64d06b46ee060e0f95c364]

Content:
Let's assume that the wheel rotates at a constant rate. Then the distance from the nut to the ground, in inches, can be modeled by a sinusoidal function [MATH: H(t),] where [MATH: t] is the time in seconds. The graph of [MATH: H(t)] is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/cc720d8d9572a60860ea9e5d9a72b24f]

Content:
Note that negative values of [MATH: H] mean the nut is under the mud.

Content:
We can obtain the following information from the graph:

Content:
- The midline is given by the line [MATH: H=10.] This means the center of the wheel is located [MATH: 10\:\textrm{cm}] above the ground.
- The nut reaches a distance of [MATH: 35 \: \textrm{cm}] above the ground at its highest point and [MATH: 15 \: \textrm{cm}] into the mud at its lowest point.
- The amplitude is [MATH: 35-10 = 25 \: \textrm{cm},] and it represents the distance from the nut to the center of the wheel.
- The period is [MATH: 5 - 1 = 4 \: \textrm{s},] and it tells us that the wheel makes one full rotation every [MATH: 4] seconds.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/2d2909b4e5799f749426b41bebc8130d]

---

Item 3 — Example: Interpreting a Sinusoidal Model From Its Graph

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/c1b6556d4ead9740e9da39b82802be35]

An object attached to the end of a spring is sliding back and forth on a frictionless surface so that its distance, in centimeters, from its starting position, can be modeled by the sinusoidal function [MATH: D(t),] where [MATH: t] is the time in seconds.

How often does the object return to its starting position?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's recall the general terminology for sinusoidal curves:

[IMG: /graphics/4ac615659a8be00387ca29d426c542a0]

The highlighted element on the graph below corresponds to the period. It represents the time difference between two consecutive maximum values:

[IMG: /graphics/d23ce87e90ae13b23d22ca4ade44d140]

From the graph, we see that the distance between the peaks (i.e., the period) is

[MATH: \textrm{period} = 2.5 - 0.5 = 2\,\textrm{seconds}.]

Therefore, the object returns to its starting position every [MATH: 2] seconds.

Item 6 — Example: Interpreting a Cosine Function

Example Prompt:
The daily tide level in a coastal city, in feet, is modeled by the function
[MATH: H(t)=6\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\right)+ 8,]
where [MATH: t] is the time in hours. How long does it take for the tide to transition from its lowest to highest level, and what is the maximum height of the tide?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's recall the general terminology for sinusoidal curves:

[IMG: /graphics/956662c08e46be57b209fa4dd4bb8837]

If [MATH: F(t) = A \cos\left( B t \right) + C,] then

- [MATH: |A|] is the amplitude,
- [MATH: \dfrac{|B|}{2\pi}] is the frequency, [MATH: \dfrac{2\pi}{|B|}] is the period, and
- [MATH: C] is the midline (vertical shift).

We'll answer each part of the question in turn.

- For the first part, we are interested in the time difference between the highest and lowest tides (i.e., half the period of the function).

Now, we have
[MATH: B = (π)/(6).]
So, the period is
[MATH: (2π)/(B)|= (2π)/(((π)/(6))); = 12hr.]
The time between the lowest and highest tides is half the period. Therefore, it takes [MATH: 6] hours for the tide to transition from its lowest to highest level.
- For the second part, we're interested in the maximum value of the function. This is given by the amplitude plus the midline.

Now, we have
[MATH: |A| = 6\,\textrm{ft}, \qquad C = 8\,\textrm{ft}.]
Therefore,
[MATH: H_{\textrm{max}} = 6\,\textrm{ft} + 8\,\textrm{ft} = 14\,\textrm{ft}.]
Therefore, the maximum height of the tide is [MATH: 14\,\textrm{ft}.]

Item 9 — Example: Interpreting a Sine Function

Example Prompt:
The altitude of a satellite [MATH: t] minutes after an astronomer starts observing it, in kilometers, is given by a function
[MATH: A(t)=8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{50}\right)+400,]
where [MATH: t] is the time in minutes. What is the difference in the satellite's altitude between the points of highest and lowest altitude?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's recall the general terminology for sinusoidal curves:

[IMG: /graphics/0c8312d732e377fd41cb68ec4c6361a8]

If [MATH: F(t) = A \sin\left( B t \right) + C,] then

- [MATH: |A|] is the amplitude,
- [MATH: \dfrac{|B|}{2\pi}] is the frequency, [MATH: \dfrac{2\pi}{|B|}] is the period, and
- [MATH: C] is the midline (vertical shift).

In our case, we are interested in the altitude difference between the highest and lowest altitude points, i.e., twice the amplitude.

Now, we have

[MATH: \text{amplitude}=|A|=8.]

Therefore, we conclude that the altitude difference is equal to

[MATH: 2\cdot {\color{black}8} = 16\,\textrm{km}.]
